content.body:
The appearance in battle, and defensive quality of, the heavier Allied tanks like the Matilda and Char.B1bis was a surprise to some German designers at the time. Combat reports from battles just waged sent them immediately back to the drawing board to develop ways to mount better guns on their tanks. The Panzer IV was fortunately equipped with a large turret ring, making the mounting of the much longer (nearly double the barrel length) 75mmL43 AT gun a simple task.
This potent weapon, coupled with a general frontal armour upgrade; made the Pz.IVg a solid performer, and a successful tank throughout the rest of the war. The original thin armor on the sides and rear left it vulnerable to flank attacks, something that Allied AT gunners would continue to use to great effect. Due to the overall anti-armour lethality of this longer 75mm gun, the Pz.IVg does not have the HEAT ammunition of its short-barreled ancestor seen in the previous Pz.IVd design.
Control Variations: almost none. Gunner sight now has a fully-modeled multi-ammo sight; PzGr is the range for AP rounds, SprGr is the range setting for HE.
The Pz.IVg became the mainstay of German armored units for the rest of the war for good reason: a highly useful combination of mobility, frontal armor, and an accurate and lethal main gun that can kill any Allied tank at significant ranges. Taken together, they make it an effective all-around weapon in any situation. Be sure to keep in mind that you have a tremendous range advantage and good quality sights. This is NOT the tank that you take down into the contested town; it is far too valuable for such a dubious role. You can sit at extended ranges, nearly impervious to frontal return fire, and annihilate any tank you see except the Churchills. Keep moving, firing, and relocating under cover wherever possible in order to minimize the ability of the enemy to focus ground or aerial resources effectively to eliminate you.
You will stand out as a particularly high-value target to Allied aircraft if they can spot you. Your commander is only useful if he is able to see; leave him unbuttoned most of the time (pull him in during air attack or if you are entering an urban area) ... if he is killed, the slight risk to your tank (through his open hatch which will then remain open) will have been more than offset by his utility to that point if you've been using him to spot enemy threats.
Move quickly from cover to cover, scanning carefully ... use shadows and brush to break up your outline as much as possible.
